## 8.1 Learning Outcome
In this chapter, we will create the followings data visualisation by using R packages:

- plotting a calender heatmap by using ggplot2 functions,
- plotting a cycle plot by using ggplot2 function,
- plotting a slopegraph
- plotting a horizon chart

## 8.2 Getting started
Firstly, we will load the following R packages: scales, viridis, lubridate, ggthemes, gridExtra, readxl, knitr, data.table and tidyverse.

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
pacman::p_load(scales, viridis, lubridate, ggthemes,
               gridExtra, readxl, knitr, data.table,
               CGPfunctions, ggHoriPlot, tidyverse)
```
:::


## 8.3 Plotting Calendar Heatmap
In this section, we will learn how to plot a calender heatmap programmatically by using ggplot2 package.
![](img/HoE8_1.png)

By the end of this section, we will:

- plot a calender heatmap by using ggplot2 functions and extension,
- write function using R programming,
- derive specific date and time related field by using base R and lubridate packages
- perform data preparation task by using tidyr and dplyr packages.

### 8.3.1 The Data
In this chapter, *eventlog.csv* file will be used. This data file consists of 199,999 rows of time-series cyber attack records by country.

### 8.3.2 Importing the data
First, we will use the code chunk below to import *eventlog.csv* file into R environment and called the data frame as *attacks*.

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
attacks <- read_csv("data/eventlog.csv")
```
:::


### 8.3.3 Examining the data structure
It is always a good practice to examine the imported data frame before further analysis is performed.

For example, *kable()* can be used to review the structure of the imported data frame.

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
kable(head(attacks))
```

::: {.cell-output-display}


|timestamp           |source_country |tz              |
|:-------------------|:--------------|:---------------|
|2015-03-12 15:59:16 |CN             |Asia/Shanghai   |
|2015-03-12 16:00:48 |FR             |Europe/Paris    |
|2015-03-12 16:02:26 |CN             |Asia/Shanghai   |
|2015-03-12 16:02:38 |US             |America/Chicago |
|2015-03-12 16:03:22 |CN             |Asia/Shanghai   |
|2015-03-12 16:03:45 |CN             |Asia/Shanghai   |


:::
:::


There are three columns, namely *timestamp, source_country* and *tz*.

- *timestamp* field stores date-time values in POSIXct format.
- *source_country* field stores the source of the attack. It is in *ISO 3166-1 alpha-2* country code.
- *tz* field stores time zone of the source IP address.

### 8.3.4 Data Preparation
Step 1: Deriving *weekday* and *hour of day* fields

Before we can plot the calender heatmap, two new fields namely *wkday* and *hour* need to be derived. In this step, we will write a function to perform the task.

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
make_hr_wkday <- function(ts, sc, tz) {
  real_times <- ymd_hms(ts, 
                        tz = tz[1], 
                        quiet = TRUE)
  dt <- data.table(source_country = sc,
                   wkday = weekdays(real_times),
                   hour = hour(real_times))
  return(dt)
  }
```
:::


::: {.callout-note}

- [`ymd_hms()`](https://lubridate.tidyverse.org/reference/ymd_hms.html) and [`hour()`](https://lubridate.tidyverse.org/reference/hour.html) are from [**lubridate**](https://lubridate.tidyverse.org/) package, and
- [`weekdays()`](https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/base/versions/3.6.2/topics/weekdays) is a **base** R function.

:::

Step 2: Deriving the attacks tibble data frame

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
wkday_levels <- c('Saturday', 'Friday', 
                  'Thursday', 'Wednesday', 
                  'Tuesday', 'Monday', 
                  'Sunday')

attacks <- attacks %>%
  group_by(tz) %>%
  do(make_hr_wkday(.$timestamp, 
                   .$source_country, 
                   .$tz)) %>% 
  ungroup() %>% 
  mutate(wkday = factor(
    wkday, levels = wkday_levels),
    hour  = factor(
      hour, levels = 0:23))
```
:::


::: {.callout-note}
Beside extracting the necessary data into *attacks* data frame, `mutate()` of **dplyr** package is used to convert *wkday* and *hour* fields into **factor** so they’ll be ordered when plotting
:::

Table below shows the tidy tibble table after processing.

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
kable(head(attacks))
```

::: {.cell-output-display}


|tz           |source_country |wkday    |hour |
|:------------|:--------------|:--------|:----|
|Africa/Cairo |BG             |Saturday |20   |
|Africa/Cairo |TW             |Sunday   |6    |
|Africa/Cairo |TW             |Sunday   |8    |
|Africa/Cairo |CN             |Sunday   |11   |
|Africa/Cairo |US             |Sunday   |15   |
|Africa/Cairo |CA             |Monday   |11   |


:::
:::


### 8.3.5 Building the Calendar Heatmaps

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
grouped <- attacks %>% 
  count(wkday, hour) %>% 
  ungroup() %>%
  na.omit()

ggplot(grouped, 
       aes(hour, 
           wkday, 
           fill = n)) + 
geom_tile(color = "white", 
          size = 0.1) + 
theme_tufte(base_family = "Helvetica") + 
coord_equal() +
scale_fill_gradient(name = "# of attacks",
                    low = "sky blue", 
                    high = "dark blue") +
labs(x = NULL, 
     y = NULL, 
     title = "Attacks by weekday and time of day") +
theme(axis.ticks = element_blank(),
      plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5),
      legend.title = element_text(size = 8),
      legend.text = element_text(size = 6) )
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](HoE8_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-7-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


::: {.callout-tip title="Things to learn from the code chunk"}

- a tibble data table called *grouped* is derived by aggregating the attack by *wkday* and *hour* fields.
- a new field called *n* is derived by using `group_by()` and `count()` functions.
- `na.omit()` is used to exclude missing value.
- `geom_tile()` is used to plot tiles (grids) at each x and y position. `color` and `size` arguments are used to specify the border color and line size of the tiles.
- [`theme_tufte()`](https://jrnold.github.io/ggthemes/reference/theme_tufte.html) of [**ggthemes**](https://jrnold.github.io/ggthemes/reference/index.html) package is used to remove unnecessary chart junk.
- `coord_equal()` is used to ensure the plot will have an aspect ratio of 1:1.
- `scale_fill_gradient()` function is used to creates a two colour gradient (low-high).

:::

Then we can simply group the count by hour and wkday and plot it, since we know that we have values for every combination there’s no need to further preprocess the data.

### 8.3.6 Building Multiple Calendar Heatmaps
**Challenge**: Building multiple heatmaps for the top four countries with the highest number of attacks.
![](img/HoE8_2.png)

### 8.3.7 Plotting Multiple Calendar Heatmaps
Step 1: Deriving attack by country object

In order to identify the top 4 countries with the highest number of attacks, we will do the followings:

- count the number of attacks by country,
- calculate the percent of attacks by country, and
- save the results in a tibble data frame.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
attacks_by_country <- count(
  attacks, source_country) %>%
  mutate(percent = percent(n/sum(n))) %>%
  arrange(desc(n))
```
:::


Step 2: Preparing the tidy data frame

In this step, we will extract the attack records of the top 4 countries from *attacks* data frame and save the data in a new tibble data frame (i.e. *top4_attacks*).

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
top4 <- attacks_by_country$source_country[1:4]
top4_attacks <- attacks %>%
  filter(source_country %in% top4) %>%
  count(source_country, wkday, hour) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(source_country = factor(
    source_country, levels = top4)) %>%
  na.omit()
```
:::


### 8.3.8 Plotting Multiple Calendar Heatmaps
Step 3: Plotting the Multiple Calender Heatmap by using ggplot2 package.

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(top4_attacks, 
       aes(hour, 
           wkday, 
           fill = n)) + 
  geom_tile(color = "white", 
          size = 0.1) + 
  theme_tufte(base_family = "Helvetica") + 
  coord_equal() +
  scale_fill_gradient(name = "# of attacks",
                    low = "sky blue", 
                    high = "dark blue") +
  facet_wrap(~source_country, ncol = 2) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, 
     title = "Attacks on top 4 countries by weekday and time of day") +
  theme(axis.ticks = element_blank(),
        axis.text.x = element_text(size = 7),
        plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5),
        legend.title = element_text(size = 8),
        legend.text = element_text(size = 6) )
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](HoE8_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-10-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


## 8.4 Plotting Cycle Plot
In this section, we will learn how to plot a cycle plot showing the time-series patterns and trend of visitor arrivals from Vietnam programmatically by using ggplot2 functions.
![](img/HoE8_3.png)

### 8.4.1 Step 1: Data Import
In this chapter, *arrivals_by_air.xlsx* will be used.

The code chunk below imports *arrivals_by_air.xlsx* by using `read_excel()` of **readxl** package and save it as a tibble data frame called *air*.

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
air <- read_excel("data/arrivals_by_air.xlsx")
```
:::


### 8.42 Step 2: Deriving month and year fields
Next, two new fields called *month* and *year* are derived from *Month-Year* field.

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
air$month <- factor(month(air$`Month-Year`), 
                    levels=1:12, 
                    labels=month.abb, 
                    ordered=TRUE) 
air$year <- year(ymd(air$`Month-Year`))
```
:::


### 8.4.3 Step 4: Extracting the target country
Next, the code chunk below is used to extract data for the target country (i.e. Vietnam)

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
Vietnam <- air %>% 
  select(`Vietnam`, 
         month, 
         year) %>%
  filter(year >= 2010)
```
:::


### 8.4.4 Step 5: Computing year average arrivals by month
The code chunk below uses `group_by()` and `summarise()` of **dplyr** to compute year average arrivals by month.

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
hline.data <- Vietnam %>% 
  group_by(month) %>%
  summarise(avgvalue = mean(`Vietnam`))
```
:::


### 8.4.5 Srep 6: Plotting the cycle plot
The code chunk below is used to plot the cycle plot.

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot() + 
  geom_line(data=Vietnam,
            aes(x=year, 
                y=`Vietnam`, 
                group=month), 
            colour="black") +
  geom_hline(aes(yintercept=avgvalue), 
             data=hline.data, 
             linetype=6, 
             colour="red", 
             size=0.5) + 
  facet_grid(~month) +
  labs(axis.text.x = element_blank(),
       title = "Visitor arrivals from Vietnam by air, Jan 2010-Dec 2019") +
  xlab("") +
  ylab("No. of Visitors") +
  theme_tufte(base_family = "Helvetica")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](HoE8_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-15-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


## 8.5 Plotting Slopegraph

In this section, we will explore how to create a **slopegraph** in R. A slopegraph is useful for comparing how values change between two time points across multiple categories. In this example, I use rice yield data to compare changes between **1961** and **1980** for selected Asian countries.

### 8.5.1 Step 1: Data Import
First, import the rice data set into the R environment.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
rice <- read_csv("data/rice.csv")
```
:::


### 8.5.2 Step 2: Preparing the data
Next, filter the data to keep only the two years of interest, namely 1961 and 1980.

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
rice_slope <- rice %>%
  mutate(Year = factor(Year)) %>%
  filter(Year %in% c(1961, 1980))
```
:::


### 8.5.3 Step 3: Plotting the slopegraph
The code chunk below creates a basic slopegraph by using ggplot2.

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="true"}
ggplot(rice_slope,
       aes(x = Year, y = Yield, group = Country)) +
  geom_line(aes(color = Country), linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(aes(color = Country), size = 2) +
  geom_text(
    data = rice_slope %>% filter(Year == 1961),
    aes(label = Country),
    hjust = 1.1,
    size = 3,
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  geom_text(
    data = rice_slope %>% filter(Year == 1980),
    aes(label = Country),
    hjust = -0.1,
    size = 3,
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  scale_x_discrete(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.2, 0.2))) +
  labs(
    title = "Rice Yield of Top 11 Asian Countries",
    subtitle = "1961-1980",
    caption = "Prepared by: Htet Kay Khaing",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Yield"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none"
  )
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](HoE8_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-18-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::
